mcq.prompt: The chapter describes three independent axes of an I/O design. Which set is it?
choices: Synchronous / asynchronous, blocking / non-blocking, local / remote
Representation (text or binary), transfer (formatted or raw), buffering (buffered or unbuffered)
Stream / stdio, locale / locale-free, checked / unchecked
Latency, throughput, durability
mcq.explain: Representation, transfer and buffering are independent choices, and each has its own cost driver: conversion work, per-value formatting, and the number of write system calls. The synchronous/blocking/remote triple describes concurrency and transport, which are real concerns but orthogonal to how bytes are produced. Deferred-format logging is what you get when you pick binary, raw and buffered on all three axes at once.

mcq.prompt: What does choosing a binary representation over text actually buy, and what does it cost?
choices: It is always smaller, and costs nothing but readability
It removes the need for buffering, at the cost of portability
It guarantees a fixed record size, at the cost of extensibility
It removes per-value conversion work, at the cost of schema, versioning and decoder obligations
mcq.explain: Text pays a conversion per value at write time; binary defers or eliminates that work but pushes an encoding contract onto both ends — someone must own the schema, its versions, and a decoder. Binary is not automatically smaller: a padded struct can easily exceed the text form of the same fields. Buffering is a separate axis and applies to both representations.

mcq.section: Streams, Buffers, and the Price of Iostreams
mcq.prompt: A helper writes `std::cout << std::hex << order_id;` and returns. What happens to output written later by unrelated code?
choices: Nothing; the manipulator applies only to the insertion it precedes
The next insertion is hexadecimal, and then the stream reverts to decimal
Every later integer insertion on std::cout is hexadecimal until something resets the base
The behaviour depends on whether the stream is tied to std::cin
mcq.explain: Base, width, precision, fill and alignment are sticky stream state, not per-insertion arguments, and std::cout is process-wide. The only per-insertion manipulator is width, which is consumed by the next formatted output; everything else persists. Saving and restoring stream.flags() contains the damage, but a self-contained std::format call avoids the shared state entirely.

mcq.section: Streams, Buffers, and the Price of Iostreams
mcq.prompt: A loop writes 100 lines with `std::cout << row << std::endl;`. What is the cost relative to using '\n'?
choices: std::endl also flushes, which can turn one batched write into a write system call per line
Identical; std::endl is spelled differently but compiles to the same thing
std::endl allocates a temporary string for the newline
std::endl is cheaper, because it lets the stream reuse its buffer
mcq.explain: std::endl inserts '\n' and then calls flush, which asks the library to push its buffer toward the operating system — defeating exactly the batching the stream buffer exists to provide. Writing '\n' lets the buffer fill and drain in whole chunks. The extra work is the flush, not any allocation.

mcq.section: Streams, Buffers, and the Price of Iostreams
mcq.prompt: Which classic stream should carry batched diagnostic output, and why?
choices: std::cerr, because it is the error stream
std::cout, because it shares the buffer with normal output
std::clog, because std::cerr has unitbuf set and flushes on every insertion
std::clog, because it writes to a different file descriptor than std::cerr
mcq.explain: std::cerr has the unitbuf flag set, so an ordinary insertion flushes eagerly — that is deliberate for a message you must see before a crash, and wasteful for a stream of diagnostics. std::clog is buffered and is the classic choice for batched logging. Both go to the same standard-error destination; the difference is flushing policy, not the descriptor.

mcq.prompt: `std::ifstream input{"ticks.csv"};` and the file does not exist. What happens by default?
choices: The constructor throws std::ios_base::failure
The constructor succeeds and the stream tests false, so you must check it
The constructor throws std::filesystem::filesystem_error
The program aborts
mcq.explain: Stream constructors do not throw on an ordinary open failure unless an exception mask was installed with .exceptions(); the failure is recorded in the state bits, so `if (!input) return {};` is mandatory. Skipping the check is how a missing file silently becomes an empty result set. Destruction still closes the handle correctly either way, since the stream owns it through RAII.

mcq.prompt: Why does the chapter's CSV reader use std::getline for transport and std::from_chars for conversion, rather than `input >> value`?
choices: Because operator>> cannot read doubles
Because getline is the only way to detect end of file
Because from_chars can read directly from a file descriptor
Because from_chars is locale-free and keeps parsing separate from transport, while stream extraction drags in locale and sticky formatting state
mcq.explain: Stream extraction consults the stream's locale for the decimal point and grouping, and it inherits whatever formatting flags a previous caller left behind — both are hazards for machine data. from_chars takes a character range, is locale-independent, and reports how far it got. Stream extraction can certainly read doubles; the objection is what it drags along while doing so.

mcq.section: C Stdio and the Two-Worlds Problem
mcq.prompt: `std::printf("%d\n", some_long)` where some_long is a `long`. What is the status of this call?
choices: It is undefined behaviour; the variadic call carries no static argument types
It prints the truncated low 32 bits, which is well-defined
It is ill-formed, since the compiler checks literal format strings
It is fine on LP64 systems where long and int have the same representation
mcq.explain: The format string is data, not a type declaration: the variadic call passes a long and %d instructs printf to read an int, which is undefined behaviour rather than a defined truncation. Compilers do warn when the format string is a literal, but a warning is a diagnostic quality-of-implementation feature, not the language making the call well-formed. On LP64 long is 8 bytes and int is 4, so they do not share a representation either.

mcq.section: C Stdio and the Two-Worlds Problem
mcq.prompt: After calling `std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false)`, what must you avoid?
choices: Using std::cin at all, since untied input can no longer block
Mixing std::printf and std::cout on the same destination and expecting program-order output
Using std::format, which relies on the synchronised buffers
Calling std::cout.flush(), which is now undefined
mcq.explain: Synchronisation is what makes the C++ and C sides share one buffering view of a destination; removing it gives each an independent buffer, so their flushes can interleave in an order unrelated to the order the calls were made. std::cin still works — the separate `std::cin.tie(nullptr)` call only removes the implicit flush of cout before each read. flush and std::format are unaffected.

mcq.prompt: What is the difference between std::format and std::println?
choices: std::format is locale-aware; std::println is not
std::format is a C++23 addition; std::println has been available since C++17
std::println can format user-defined types; std::format cannot
std::format returns a std::string; std::println writes formatted output plus a newline to stdout or a FILE*
mcq.explain: std::format (C++20) produces an owning string the caller then does something with; std::print and std::println (C++23) send the formatted characters straight to a destination and skip the intermediate string. Both are locale-independent by default and both use the same std::formatter machinery, so a user-defined formatter works with either.

mcq.prompt: `std::format("{:d}", "text")` — what happens?
choices: It prints the address of the string literal in decimal
It throws std::format_error at runtime
It is ill-formed: a literal format string is checked at compile time against its argument types
It formats the string and ignores the unusable 'd' specifier
mcq.explain: A literal format string is a consteval-checked object, so the mismatch between the integer presentation type 'd' and a string argument is reported at compile time — the whole reason to prefer format over printf. std::format_error is the runtime failure mode, and it applies to format strings supplied at runtime, which must go through std::vformat and cannot get the compile-time check.

mcq.prompt: What does `std::format("{:*>8.2f}", 201.25)` produce?
choices: "201.25" followed by two spaces
mcq.explain: Read the spec left to right: `*` is the fill character, `>` means right-align, `8` is the field width, `.2` is the precision and `f` is fixed notation. 201.25 renders as six characters, so two fill characters pad it on the left. Getting `<` and `>` backwards is the usual slip — `>` pushes the text to the right, so the padding lands on the left.

mcq.prompt: A format string is read from a configuration file at startup. Which statement is correct?
choices: Pass it to std::format directly; the check is only skipped for non-literals
Runtime format strings are rejected outright and must be converted to literals
std::format silently ignores replacement fields it cannot validate
It cannot receive the compile-time check; use std::vformat with std::make_format_args, and be ready for std::format_error
mcq.explain: std::format's parameter is a consteval-constructed format string, so a runtime std::string does not satisfy it — the code will not compile rather than silently skipping the check. std::vformat takes an unchecked format string with type-erased arguments and throws std::format_error when parsing fails, which becomes an ordinary error path you must handle. C++26's std::runtime_format is a convenience spelling for the same thing.

mcq.prompt: `std::format_to_n(begin, 8, "price={:.2f}", 101.25)` — what do the two members of the returned result mean?
choices: `out` is the number of characters written and `size` is the buffer capacity
Both report 8, since that is the limit
`size` is the number of characters the complete output required (12 here); `out` marks the end of what was actually written
`size` is the number of characters written and `out` points at the null terminator
mcq.explain: format_to_n writes at most n characters but still reports the full size the output would have needed, which is what lets the caller detect truncation with `result.size > capacity`. Reading `size` as the written count is the dangerous misreading: it turns an overflow into a silently accepted partial record. No terminator is written, so the caller must carry the length itself.

mcq.prompt: When is `std::formatted_size(fmt, args...)` followed by `std::format_to` the right shape, and when is it not?
choices: Always, since it produces exactly one allocation
Never; it is strictly slower than std::format
It suits a cold path that wants one exactly sized allocation, but not a hot path, because it processes the format twice
It suits a hot path, because sizing is free at compile time
mcq.explain: formatted_size performs the whole format pass just to count characters, so the write pass repeats that work — one exact allocation bought with double the conversion cost. That trade makes sense on a cold path building a large message; on a hot path with a known upper bound, format_to_n into fixed caller-owned storage does the job in one pass. The sizing is a runtime computation, not a compile-time one.

mcq.prompt: A service formats prices with `stream << value` and is deployed to a host whose locale renders 42.5 as "42,5". A downstream parser breaks. What is the correct diagnosis?
choices: Classic-stream numeric output is locale-dependent, so machine-consumed output should use locale-free conversion such as std::format or std::to_chars
The downstream parser is wrong to assume a decimal point
The host's locale data is corrupt
The stream needed a wider precision setting
mcq.explain: Both programs were individually obeying their locale settings; the defect is that a machine-to-machine interface was routed through a human-presentation facility at all. std::format is locale-independent by default, and to_chars/from_chars are locale-free, which makes the bytes identical on every host. Localisation should be an explicit opt-in at the point where a human reads the output.

mcq.prompt: Under the default "C" locale, what does classic-stream numeric output still pay for?
choices: Nothing; the "C" locale short-circuits the locale machinery entirely
Only a single branch checking whether the locale is "C"
A full string allocation per formatted value
Facet lookup and virtual conversion calls, which remain part of the path
mcq.explain: The stream still consults its imbued locale's num_put facet through a virtual call and applies grouping and decimal-point rules — the "C" locale makes those rules trivial, not absent. That residual machinery is one of the reasons a std::format call is cheaper for the same output. Constructing std::locale{""} is a separate hazard: it reads the environment and can throw std::runtime_error for a locale the host does not have installed.

mcq.prompt: Why is `while (!input.eof()) { input >> value; use(value); }` wrong?
choices: eofbit is only set for file streams, never for string streams
End of file is discovered by attempting a read, so the last iteration processes a value the extraction never produced
eof() clears the failbit as a side effect
It is correct, but slower than the extraction-in-condition form
mcq.explain: eofbit is set as a consequence of a read that ran out of input, so the flag is still clear when the final, failing extraction is attempted — the loop body then runs once more on a value the stream did not write. `while (input >> value)` tests the extraction itself and stops on either malformed input or exhaustion. eof() has no side effects; it only reports the bit.

mcq.prompt: A stream's failbit is set by a malformed token. What must happen before extraction can resume?
choices: Nothing; the next extraction retries automatically
The stream must be closed and reopened
Call .clear() to reset the state, then consume the offending characters
Call .exceptions(std::ios::failbit) so the failure surfaces as an exception
mcq.explain: Once a failure bit is set, later operations do nothing until the state is reset — and clearing alone is not enough, because the offending characters are still sitting in the stream and will fail the same way. The chapter's recovery reads the bad token into a std::string to consume it. Installing an exception mask changes how the failure is reported, not how the input is resynchronised.

mcq.section: Asynchronous Logging: Formatting Off the Hot Path
mcq.prompt: In the chapter's deferred-format design, what does the hot-path `log_event` actually do?
choices: Reads a steady_clock timestamp and stores fixed-size fields plus a site id into an already-allocated slot
Formats a short message and appends it to a preallocated string
Enqueues a std::string built with std::format so the consumer only writes
Writes the record with fwrite to a buffered FILE* so no system call happens
mcq.explain: The producer's entire job is one clock read and a few fixed-size stores into storage the constructor already allocated — no formatting, no allocation, no output system call. The consumer maps the site id to a format schema and pays the conversion cost off the critical path. Storing a formatted or arbitrary-length string in the event is the pitfall the design exists to avoid: it reintroduces allocation and variable-size copying on the hot thread.

reading.section: Streams, Buffers, and the Price of Iostreams
reading.explain: Almost every stream manipulator is sticky, and exactly one of the ones here is not: width is consumed by the next formatted output and resets to zero, while fill and precision stay until something changes them. So 42 is padded to six characters with dots, 7 is printed with no padding at all, and both doubles are rendered at three significant digits — 3.14 and 2.72, the second rounded. The tempting reading is that setw(6) sets a column width for the line, which is how every other manipulator behaves and how the name reads; a table built this way silently loses its alignment from the second column on. Re-apply setw before each field, or use std::format, where the width belongs to one replacement field and nothing leaks.

The library does not pad anything on a formatter's behalf. It hands the replacement field's specification to that type's parse and then hands the output iterator to its format; whatever appears between the braces means only what the formatter chooses to do with it. This parse swallows `>8` without recording it, so the temperature is written unpadded, while the identical spec applied to a string goes through the standard formatter and is right-aligned in eight columns. The tempting reading is that width and alignment are applied by std::format around the result, so any type gets them for free — they are not, and a custom formatter that ignores its spec produces a table that only misaligns on the custom column. Deriving from std::formatter<std::string> and delegating is how a type inherits the whole alignment vocabulary.

The complete text is `user=amelia id=7`, sixteen characters, and result.size reports that full required length whether or not it fitted — that is the whole point of the return value, since comparing it against the capacity is how overflow becomes a visible branch. Only twelve characters were written, so result.out sits at the end of the buffer and the written prefix stops mid-record, after the space. The tempting reading is that result.size is what was written, which makes an overflowing record look successful and, worse, invites indexing with it; note too that nothing appended a terminator, so the length must be carried separately rather than recovered by scanning for a zero byte.

The extraction of `x` into an int fails, setting failbit but not eofbit — the stream stopped on a character it could not use, not at the end — hence 1 and 0. Until clear() resets the state every further operation is a no-op, so recovery has two parts: clear the flags *and* consume the token that caused the failure, otherwise the next attempt meets the same `x` and the loop spins forever. After that, 9 extracts successfully, and reading it consumed the last character, so eofbit is set while failbit is not: the final columns are 0 and 1. The tempting reading is that eof() is the way to ask whether input is exhausted before reading — end of file is discovered by attempting a read, and here eof() is still false at a point where nothing more can be extracted as an int.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: std::format takes a std::format_string, which is constructed from its argument at compile time and checks the braces against the argument types right there. A std::string variable is not a constant expression, so there is nothing to check and the conversion is rejected — the error is about the format string parameter, not about the 2 and the 5. That checking is the feature: a mismatch such as `{:d}` against text becomes a compile error rather than a runtime throw. The tempting reading is that a format string is just a string, as it is in printf, so any std::string should do; when the pattern genuinely arrives at runtime, pass it through std::vformat with std::make_format_args, and be ready for the std::format_error that parsing can now throw.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: format_to writes through an output iterator and never learns where that iterator's storage ends — the destination is what decides the bounds, and a raw pointer into a 16-byte array decides nothing. The text needs 26 characters, so the last ten are written past the end of the array, which the address sanitizer reports as a stack-buffer-overflow. The tempting reading is that a fixed-size destination bounds the write, or that the array's zero-initialisation leaves room; the size is known to the array, not to the iterator handed over. format_to_n is the bounded sibling: it takes the capacity as an argument and reports the length the record actually needed, turning overflow into a branch the caller writes.

writing.section: Streams, Buffers, and the Price of Iostreams
writing.prompt: Write `hexdump_row(std::ostream& out, std::span<const std::uint8_t> bytes)` printing each byte as exactly two lowercase hex digits, separated by single spaces. Contract: `std::format` may not be used, and the caller's next unrelated insertion must be formatted exactly as it would have been had this function never run.
checklist: Saves and restores the stream's fmtflags and fill character
Restoration happens on every exit path (RAII guard, or a single exit point)
setw is re-applied for every byte, because width is not sticky
Each byte is widened to unsigned (or int) before insertion, so uint8_t is not printed as a character
The separator logic emits no trailing space
writing.notes: The same output with std::format is `out << std::format("{:02x}", byte)` and needs no guard at all, because the specification lives in the replacement field and nothing survives the call -- that contrast is the reason to write the guard once and then stop reaching for manipulators. Note that copyfmt copies the whole formatting state including the locale and the exception mask, which is more than this needs and is not free.

writing.prompt: Write `load_thresholds(std::istream&)` returning `std::map<std::string, double>` for a config of `name = value` lines, ignoring blank lines and everything after a `#`. Contract: numeric conversion must be locale-independent and must reject a field with trailing junk; a file saved on Windows must parse identically; and no std::stringstream may be constructed anywhere.
checklist: Transport is std::getline; conversion is std::from_chars
A trailing '\r' is stripped, so CRLF files parse the same as LF files
Comments are removed before the '=' is located, so a '#' cannot be mistaken for data
The from_chars result is checked for both an error code and for reaching the end of the field
No std::stringstream, std::stod, or std::atof anywhere
writing.notes: from_chars is the locale-free layer, which is what keeps a host configured for a comma decimal separator from reading 1.5 as 1. A stringstream per line would work and is what most code does; it constructs a full iostream, consults the locale, and may allocate -- for a config read once at startup that is affordable, and for anything that runs per record it is the thing to remove first.

writing.prompt: `struct Bytes { std::uint64_t count; };` should format as `900 B`, `1.5 KiB` or `2.0 MiB`. Write its `std::formatter` specialization. Contract: `std::format("{:>10}|", Bytes{1536})` must right-align the rendered text in ten columns, and your formatter must not implement padding, alignment or fill itself.
checklist: The specialization derives from std::formatter<std::string> (or another standard formatter) rather than writing parse from scratch
parse is inherited, so the whole standard alignment vocabulary works
format builds the rendered text, then delegates to the base class's format
The unit selection divides by 1024, not 1000, and stops at the largest applicable unit
format is a const member function
writing.notes: Writing parse by hand and returning context.begin() looks harmless until someone passes a specification: the parser must consume up to the closing brace, and with a literal format string a leftover specification is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise. If the type deserves its own vocabulary -- say `{:b}` for raw bytes versus `{:h}` for human units -- that is when a hand-written parse earns its keep, and it should still delegate the alignment part.

writing.prompt: An audit trail stores fixed-size rows: `struct Row { std::array<char, 64> bytes; std::size_t size; bool truncated; };`. Write `make_row(std::string_view actor, std::string_view action, std::int64_t object_id)` returning a filled `Row`. Contract: no allocation, never a write past the array, and truncation must be recorded rather than reported as failure — the audit trail would rather keep a clipped row than none.
checklist: Uses std::format_to_n with the array's size as the bound
size is computed from result.out, not from result.size
truncated is set by comparing result.size against the array's capacity
No std::string, std::format or other allocating call appears
A comment states that no terminator is written, so size is the record boundary
writing.notes: The other policy -- refuse the row and return nothing -- is equally defensible and is the right one for a record a decoder must parse in full; what is never defensible is silently keeping a clipped row without saying so, because the truncation then looks like data. Note that a std::string_view argument can be arbitrarily long, so the bound here is doing real work rather than guarding a theoretical case.

writing.prompt: A receipt file mixes prices with words. Write `total(std::istream&)` returning `std::pair<double, int>` — the sum of every value that parsed as a number, and the count of tokens that did not. Contract: it must terminate on any input, including one containing no numbers at all, and it must not treat a device error as end of input.
checklist: The extraction and the loop condition are the same operation
After a failed extraction the state is cleared *and* the offending token is consumed
eof and bad are distinguished from a plain parse failure, and bad ends the loop
The skip count counts tokens, not characters
No call to eof() is used as the loop condition
writing.notes: Reaching for .exceptions(failbit) here would turn every ordinary bad token into a thrown exception on what is really a parsing loop -- the state-bit style fits partial input precisely because most of these failures are expected. The eof/bad split matters more than it looks: a truncated read from a failing disk and a clean end of file both stop the loop, but only one of them means the total is complete.

writing.section: Asynchronous Logging: Formatting Off the Hot Path
writing.prompt: Build the two halves of a deferred-format logger for a game frame loop. `FrameLog::record(site, a, b)` runs inside the frame and `FrameLog::drain(std::FILE*)` runs between frames. Contract: `record` is noexcept, performs no formatting, no allocation and no system call, and a full buffer must be counted rather than dropped silently; `drain` must perform at most one allocation in total, however many events it writes.
checklist: The event is a fixed-size POD-like struct: an id, numeric fields and a timestamp — no std::string
Storage is allocated once in the constructor; record writes into an existing slot rather than push_back
record is noexcept and a full buffer increments a dropped counter that the caller can read
drain formats into one reused std::string (clear plus format_to on a back_inserter), not a fresh string per event
drain resets the buffer so the next frame starts empty
writing.notes: Storing the site id rather than a message is what keeps the event fixed-size; the cost is a decoder obligation, since the mapping from id to format string now lives somewhere else and has to be versioned with the log. The dropped counter is the honest half of a bounded buffer: an unbounded one would turn sustained overload into memory growth instead, and choosing between blocking, dropping and sampling is a policy the system has to state rather than inherit.
